notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes for Job 2, drawn from the sources accessed across the approved traditions.

---

## Job 2:1-3 — The Second Heavenly Council

**v. 1:** The scene closely mirrors Job 1:6. The Pulpit Commentary notes that there is no Hebrew word for "again" — the wording is an exact repetition of the former passage, but marks a second occasion. It adds that here Satan "came also among them **to present himself before the Lord**" — additional wording suggesting that whereas on the first occasion Satan came merely to observe, now he anticipated a colloquy and was prepared to answer. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/2.htm) Gill notes that Satan came either by summons or willingly, seeking opportunity to accuse Job afresh and get his commission enlarged. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/2.htm) David Guzik (Enduring Word) comments that the dialogue "was completely unknown to Job; though perhaps, if he was the author of the book, at a later time God revealed this heavenly behind-the-scenes conversation to him." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-2/)

**v. 2:** The exchange is almost identical to 1:7. Satan describes himself as "going to and fro in the earth, and from walking up and down in it." Spurgeon commented: "Full of evil as Satan is, he is not idle. A lazy man commits one more sin than the devil himself." (https://www.studylight.org/daily-devotionals/eng/mae/02-02.html) The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary adds that Satan roams "like a caged lion or tiger … seeking whom he may devour" (cf. 1 Peter 5:8). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/job-2.html)

**v. 3:** God repeats His boast about Job — but with a crucial addition: **"and still he holds fast his integrity, although you incited Me against him, to destroy him without cause."** The Pulpit Commentary calls "still he holdeth fast his integrity" the "key-note of the whole book" (Cook). God declares with His own mouth that Satan's first assault failed: Job's integrity was not wrested from him. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/2.htm)

- **"You incited Me against him"**: Guzik (Enduring Word) explains that "both God and Satan understood that the attack could only come to Job because God allowed it." God did not actively send the raiders and disasters, but they could only come by His permission. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-2/) John Piper (Desiring God) emphasizes the same sovereignty point: "God saying, 'I did it. You incited me against my boy, and I did it without reason.'" Yet Piper explains "without cause" does not mean "without purpose" — there was no sinful cause *in Job* that prompted the calamities, but God did have purposes. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/job-when-the-righteous-suffer-part-1)

- **"Without cause"**: Gill explains the Hebrew can carry the sense "in vain" — Satan's calumny against Job was not supported by any evidence, and in the end Job did not prove to be the man Satan claimed he was. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/2.htm) Guzik concurs: no sinful cause existed in Job; the "cause" lay in what God and Satan each sought to prove. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-2/)

---

## Job 2:4-6 — Satan's Second Challenge

**v. 4 — "Skin for skin"**: This is a proverbial expression. The Pulpit Commentary explains: Satan means that to keep his own "skin" intact, a man will sacrifice another's skin — even that of his nearest and dearest. Job, Satan insinuates, submitted to the loss of his children without a murmur only because he feared God would otherwise strike his own person. Satan "cannot imagine any motive for submission and apparent resignation but a selfish one." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/2.htm) Ellicott calls it "a more extreme form of the insinuation of Job 1:9. He means Job takes care to have his *quid pro quo*." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-2.html)

Guzik (Enduring Word) cites Lawson: "In Job's ancient culture, 'skin for skin' was a bartering term meaning to trade one skin for another. The Devil is accusing Job of being willing to risk the skin of his children and livestock in order to protect his own skin." Guzik adds: "There is certainly some truth to the statement, *all that a man has he will give for his life*" — he notes Abraham betrayed his wife to save his life, David feigned insanity, and Peter denied Jesus. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-2/)

Gill offers a detailed alternative reading: "skin upon skin" or "skin within skin," referring to the two layers of human skin (cutis and cuticula). A man will part with both, enduring the most exquisite torment, rather than part with his life. But Gill argues Satan's deeper insinuation is that any man — and so Job — "would part with his God, and his religion, and the profession of it, for the sake of it, which is false." Good men "reckon the loving kindness of God better than life." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/2.htm)

The Precept Austin devotional notes that Satan's motto would be: "When the going gets tough, the 'tough' desert God." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/job_devotionals-2)

**v. 5 — "Touch his bone and his flesh"**: Satan insists that if calamity comes upon Job's own body, Job will curse God to His face. Guzik quotes Morgan: "It is the devil's perpetual estimate of humanity that flesh is supreme." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-2/) Spurgeon noted: "Satan suggested that bodily pain would be the weapon to wound Job's faith; yea, and turn it into rebellion. There was much malicious cunning in this, for many a man has yielded before the miseries of physical pain though he had been proof against every other trial." (https://www.studylight.org/daily-devotionals/eng/mae/02-02.html) Gill notes that the Hebrew verb can be read "he will bless thee" — a euphemism or sarcasm, meaning "he will take his farewell of thee," having nothing more to do with God or religion. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/2.htm)

**v. 6 — "He is in your hands, but you must spare his life"**: God again lowers the protective hedge but does not eliminate it. Guzik: "Satan was given greater allowance to attack Job, but not unlimited allowance." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-2/) Ellicott notes: "God's faithfulness cannot fail even if, as Satan hints, Job's should do so (2 Timothy 2:13). There was one who cared for Job's life more than he cared for it himself." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-2.html) The Pulpit Commentary adds a rationale: the didactic purposes for which God allowed Job to be tried "would have been frustrated by Job's removal from the earth." The lesson of Job's example to future generations would have been lost. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/2.htm)

Piper (Desiring God) underscores God's sovereignty: "He says, 'Thus far and no farther you may go. I draw the lines for Satan everywhere he goes. I pull him back and I let him out. He's never free from my sovereign rule.'" (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/job-when-the-righteous-suffer-part-1)

---

## Job 2:7-8 — Job Afflicted with Boils

**v. 7:** "So Satan went out from the presence of the LORD and infected Job with terrible boils from the soles of his feet to the crown of his head." Ellicott identifies the disease as possibly elephantiasis, "an extreme form of leprosy, in which the skin becomes clotted and hard like an elephant's, with painful cracks and sores underneath." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-2.html) Constable suggests "pemphigus foliaceous or something similar to it, perhaps elephantiasis." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/job-2.html) Guzik, citing Andersen, says: "Some kind of acute dermatitis spreading everywhere and developing infections with darkened (Job 30:28) and peeling (30:30) skin and constantly erupting pustules (7:5b) would manifest the pruritus and purulence highlighted in 2:7." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-2/)

Gill emphasizes the severity: it was "the worst" boil — they stood so thick and close together they were as one, reaching from head to foot, with no part free. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/2.htm) Guzik catalogues the symptoms gathered from later chapters: intense pain, peeling and darkened skin, pus-filled erupting sores, emaciation, fever, depression, weeping, sleeplessness, nightmares, putrid breath, difficulty breathing, failing vision, rotting teeth, and haggard looks — a condition lasting months (Job 7:3; 29:2). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-2/)

Guzik also notes that this passage shows Satan has power to attack mankind through disease — citing Luke 13:16 where Jesus says a woman was "bound by Satan" for 18 years with a spirit of infirmity. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-2/)

**v. 8:** Job takes a piece of broken pottery to scrape himself and sits among the ashes. Guzik suggests "in the midst of the ashes" probably means the city dump where garbage was burned. Poole (cited by Guzik) says the potsherd was "partly to allay the itch which his ulcers caused; and partly to squeeze out or take away that purulent matter which was under them." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-2/) The Pulpit Commentary says the ashes were not for curative purposes but were "simply as was the custom of mourners" (citing Isaiah 47:3; 58:5; Jeremiah 6:26; Ezekiel 27:30; Jonah 3:6). It notes the LXX rendering "on the dung-heap" is "highly improbable." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/2.htm) Gill adds that ashes were used dry as an abstersive for ulcers and that Galen noted their use in fresh wounds to stop bleeding. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/2.htm)

---

## Job 2:9-10 — Job's Wife and Job's Response

**v. 9 — "Do you still retain your integrity? Curse God and die!"**: The Pulpit Commentary observes that Job's wife had been silent through the earlier calamities but "now she can endure no longer. To see her husband so afflicted, and so patient under his afflictions, is more than she can bear. Her mind is weak and ill regulated, and she suffers herself to become Satan's ally and her husband's worst enemy." Notably, she urges Job to do exactly what Satan predicted he would do. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/2.htm)

Guzik, however, urges some restraint in judging her: "She also lost her children and her wealth and should not be too harshly judged." He cites the expanded Septuagint version where her speech is much longer, expressing her own grief as a mother who bore children "in vain." He then notes: "Satan's goal in his attacks against Job was to shake Job from his standing; he failed in regard to Job, but he succeeded in regard to Job's wife." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-2/)

Ellicott comments: "Thus it is that a man's foes are they of his own household (Micah 7:6; Matthew 10:36). The worst trial of all is when those nearest to us, instead of strengthening our hand in God and confirming our faith, conspire to destroy it." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-2.html)

**v. 10 — Job's reply: "You speak as a foolish woman speaks … Should we accept from God only good and not adversity?"**: Guzik highlights Job's pastoral wisdom and gentleness: "He did not accuse her of *being* a foolish woman, but of *speaking like* one of the foolish women. He indicated that this was out of character for her." He also notes Job's deep principle: "even affliction can be a gift to receive, not a curse to curse back." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-2/)

The Pulpit Commentary explains that *nabal* (foolish) here means not mere natural folly but "that perversion of the intellect which comes on men when their hearts and understandings are corrupted and degraded" (cf. 2 Samuel 13:13; Psalm 14:1). Job asks: would it be fair to take all the good things as a matter of course and then murmur when evil comes? Yet the commentary judges that Job had "perhaps, scarcely attained to the conviction that whatever God sends to his faithful servants is always that which is best for them — that afflictions, in fact, are blessings in disguise." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/2.htm)

Ellicott sees more in the words than Job himself realized: "merely to receive evil as from God's hands is to transmute its character altogether, for then even calamities become blessings in disguise." He draws a "sublime contrast between the temptation of Job and the temptation of Christ (Matthew 26:39-42)." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-2.html)

Piper (Desiring God) emphasizes the sovereignty theology: Job knows Satan is on a leash and "he's looking right through the immediate cause up to the ultimate cause and saying, 'Shall we receive good at the hand of the Lord and not receive evil?'" Piper notes the inspired narrator's endorsement: "In all this Job did not sin with his lips." This authorial comment confirms that "when Job affirms that good and evil, health and disease come from the hand of God, he's not sinning; he's speaking the way we ought to speak." (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/job-when-the-righteous-suffer-part-1)

**"In all this, Job did not sin in what he said"**: Guzik notes this is a "remarkable statement to the credit of Job" and uses it to counter word-of-faith teaching: "some say that these calamities came upon Job because of a negative confession he made, supposedly recorded in Job 1:5 and in Job 3:25. This statement makes it clear that Job did not sin with his lips, certainly not in the sense of a negative confession." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-2/)

---

## Job 2:11-13 — The Arrival of the Three Friends

**v. 11:** Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite come. Ellicott notes that Teman was the son of Eliphaz, son of Esau (Genesis 36:4, 10-11), and its inhabitants "were famed for their wisdom" (Jeremiah 49:7). Bildad probably derived from Shuah, son of Abraham by Keturah (Genesis 25:2). Zophar's origin is unknown. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-2.html)

The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary characterizes the three friends: Eliphaz as "a dogmatist," Bildad as "a traditionalist," and Zophar as "a know-all-dogmatist." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/job-2.html)

Guzik notes that "they had made an appointment together" shows they were already acquaintances who felt it better to come together. Their goal was good: "to come and mourn with him, and to comfort him." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-2/)

The Pulpit Commentary observes it was probably some weeks or months before news reached them, then they communicated and agreed on a time. Some months (at least two) seem to have elapsed before their arrival (cf. Job 7:3). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/2.htm)

**v. 12:** When they saw Job from a distance, they could not recognize him — his disease had so disfigured him. They wept aloud, tore their robes, and threw dust into the air over their heads. These are traditional Oriental mourning gestures. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/2.htm) Ellicott contrasts this with Luke 15:20, where the father *could* recognize his lost son despite his degradation. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-2.html)

**v. 13 — The seven-day silence:** The friends sat with Job on the ground for seven days and seven nights without speaking, "for they saw that his grief was very great." The Pulpit Commentary says the seven days was "appropriate to mournings" (cf. Genesis 50:10; 1 Samuel 31:13) and explains the long silence as an Oriental custom: "it is a point of decorum, and one dictated by a fine and true feeling, not to speak to a person in deep affliction until he gives an intimation of a desire to be comforted" (Cook). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/2.htm)

Guzik calls this "a wonderful display of comfort and common cause with Job. They shared in his afflicted state, acting as if they were similarly afflicted. They offered no statement except for their compassionate presence." He notes that the 35 chapters of debate to follow must be read against this backdrop of "genuine love and concern." Morgan (cited by Guzik) says the friends are to be admired because they came, they wept, they sat in silence for seven days, they intended the best, and they spoke *to* Job rather than about him to others. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-2/)

The Precept Austin devotional draws a pastoral application: "Sometimes there really isn't anything that can be said. Sometimes the best thing we can do is to sit silently with those who suffer and allow ourselves to enter into their pain. Sometimes our silent presence is our best and most caring ministry." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/job_devotionals-2)

Ellicott remarks: "There is a colossal grandeur about this description which is in keeping with the majesty and hoary antiquity of the poem." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-2.html)

---

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

**Reformed / Sovereign Grace (Piper, Desiring God):** John Piper emphasizes God's absolute sovereignty over suffering. God permits Satan to act, but Satan is always on a leash. The inspired narrator's verdict — "in all this Job did not sin with his lips" — provides the normative theological lens: it is *right* to say both good and calamity come from God's hand. Piper also notes (from his broader teaching on Job) that suffering serves two basic purposes: (1) to display the worth of God in the allegiance of His suffering people (chs. 1–2), and (2) to purge remaining pride (the Elihu theme). (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/holding-on-to-your-faith-in-the-midst-of-suffering-job) and (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/job-when-the-righteous-suffer-part-1)

**Baptist (Spurgeon, Garner-Howes):** Spurgeon reads Satan's presence among the "sons of God" as a warning about church assemblies: "Even the devil will attend divine worship to serve his own ends. It is, therefore, a poor confidence which looks for salvation because church or chapel have been regularly attended." He also notes Satan's strategy in using Job's wife: "Satan tried to ruin Job through her who should have been his best comforter, but he was defeated, for he only led Job to utter another of those notable speeches which are now the treasures of the church." (https://www.studylight.org/daily-devotionals/eng/mae/02-02.html) The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary identifies the friends as dogmatist, traditionalist, and know-all-dogmatist, and emphasizes that Satan "lied, being the father of lies" (John 8:44) when he said "skin for skin." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/job-2.html)

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / Guzik):** David Guzik explicitly counters word-of-faith / "positive confession" teaching by pointing to v. 10: "This statement makes it clear that Job did not sin with his lips, certainly not in the sense of a negative confession." This is a direct rebuttal to prosperity-gospel teachers who claim Job's suffering was caused by his own negative words. Guzik also emphasizes Satan's real power to cause physical disease (citing Luke 13:16). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-2/)

**Anglican (Ellicott):** Ellicott draws a typological / Christological connection: "There is a sublime contrast between the temptation of Job and the temptation of Christ" — Job's patient reception of evil from God's hand foreshadows but is surpassed by Christ's obedience in Gethsemane. He also emphasizes the moral dimension: "merely to receive evil as from God's hands is to transmute its character altogether, for then even calamities become blessings in disguise." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-2.html)

---

## Other Views

**On the nature of Job's disease:** Traditional commentary (Ellicott, Constable) leans toward elephantiasis or pemphigus foliaceous. Gill notes fourteen different diseases have been attributed to Job by various scholars, one even suggesting smallpox. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/2.htm) and (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/job-2.html)

**Catholic and Orthodox readings:** Searches to Catholic (newadvent.org, catholic.com) and Orthodox (oca.org) sources could not be completed within the available search limit. The LXX rendering "on the dung-heap" (v. 8) is noted by the Pulpit Commentary but judged "highly improbable." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/2.htm)

**Word of Faith / Prosperity teaching (debated):** Guzik's commentary explicitly rebuts the teaching that Job's calamities were caused by a "negative confession." He cites Job 1:5 and 3:25 as verses sometimes used this way, but argues that the narrator's statement in 2:10 — "in all this Job did not sin with his lips" — flatly contradicts the claim that Job's words brought on his suffering. No direct positive source for prosperity teaching on Job 2 was retrieved within the search limit. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-2/)
